This game.

This game isn't like most hacking simulators. While it certainly bears a lot of similarities to Uplink, the two games are quite different under the surface. Where Uplink is a sandbox, where the net is your playground, Hacknet is a more focused, and much deeper experience.

It is essentially a text based adventure game, but instead of typing actions your character does, you type commands into the console to hack stuff. It's intuitive and very fun to use once you get the hang of it, and the game does a good job of making you use it in intuitive and challenging ways.

The game also has a more graphic interface (which can be customised with various skins, once you learn how), and some things are only possible through using that, but I'd very much recommend you get used to the console command (trust me, you'll need them).

So what's the game about? To put it simply, it's about following a trail of websites and databases to uncover a mystery; you do this by compromising various systems through a robust hacking system and doing contracts for various hacker groups. It's not just about hacking, though, as you'll then have to search through the system's files to accomplish what you came for, whether it's deleting or editing a file, crashing a website, or browsing through the user's mails and documents to find a clue or a loophole through a heavily defended system. It's very fun and just as much a test of your deductive abilities as your hacking skills. The final mission especially left me stumped and unable to progress, until I realized I could use a technique that I had learned at the start of the game to find a loophole and break through.

But what really sold this game for me was the atmosphere and the story. The game does a really good job of making you feel immersed in the role of a hacker, and I could feel my heart pounding when I disconnected from a system a split second before getting traced, or when I had to hack into my ISP to change my IP-address before I got discovered. You feel like a goddamn badass when you manage to breach a difficult system, or when you engage in some sweet revenge on a rival hacker. The game also left me agonizing over choices that I barely would have given a thought in other games (Two words: Project Juneburg).

The story is very well done. While it borrows some themes from Uplink, it executes them very well, and I may have felled a little tear at the ending.

All in all, if you like any of the things I mentioned, you should definitely give this game a try. This was probably one of my favorite games of 2015, and it's well worth the money.

[h1] The Story [/h1]

First of all, I didn't even expect a hacking game to have a deep story (or even have one). How wrong I was.
When you launch a game, you start by receiving a message from Bit, telling that he's already dead if you read this, and then asking you some requests.
So you just do what he wants, without really knowing why, but hey, you're doing a dead man's last requests.
After some hacking and deleting stuff, he'll told you that he hasn't the time to learn you more, and that you have to join a small group of hackers.
Then you'll just complete some contracts, eventually acquiring some new hacking tools and learning more on how to hack things, to finally join another group of hackers, but more experienced and related to Bit.
You'll complete some more contracts, until someone contacts you about Bit and his disappearance, asking you to help him to investigate this. 

So the game is basically a succession of contracts/missions, but each of them has its short but not uninteresting story.
For example, you'll have to hack the server of a company in order to delete a file they asked a hacker to get, or you'll need to hack a school server to add a degree for someone, hack the personal computer of a scientist to see if he's not working on a personal project, etc ...
Special mention for the Junebug Project (seriously, do that one, because yes, you don't have to do all the contracts to progress in the story).

Also don't forget to read the logs in /home folders, there are a lot of funny hidden things ;)

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

The game is very pleasant to play and easy to take in hand, but also very fun. Basically, you just run programs to open ports to be able to hack. Of course, there are plenty of other things to do, but I won't tell you everything, otherwise it won't be fun for you :p
So while progressing in the game, you will obtain more tools to be able to hack more sophisticated and protected machines, but the more things you'll have to do, the more time it will take, and sometimes, you don't have time because you're traced, so you have to deal with everything you know to be as fast as possible and to succeed in your mission.

[h1] Soundtrack [/h1]

The soundtrack of this game is really amazing, it can be relaxing when you're doing easy contracts or pressing when you're in a hurry, it adapts very well during the game.
Shout-out for the last mission with this absolute masterpiece from Carpenter Brut : Roller Mobster.
Bit by Chris Larkin is also a very good one, but they all are :p
Also, this soundtrack reminds me a bit the Hotline Miami soundtrack, in the style, and that's a good point for me.


[h1] Pros [/h1]

[*] Very cool and deep story
[*] Pleasant gameplay, plus easy to take in hand
[*] Awesome soundtrack
[*] Interesting contracts/missions

[h1] Cons [/h1]

[*] There are still some bugs, like missions not starting, but it's not frequent (happened to me once)
[*] A little short, but for the price it's ok. You can still start a new game and do the contracts you didn't, plus there's an alternate way to do the game ;)

Hacknet is "an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator" where you'll use real UNIX commands. After being accepted by hacking guilds, you'll be working on different contracts to infiltrate networks. To access networks, you’ll open ports, bypass firewalls, overload proxy servers, finish your job before you get traced and cover your tracks when done. You’ll even scan personel computers to find mobile devices and extend your network map.

Each contract you take has its own tale and each network you connect holds different documents to explore. Besides the necessary objective file, most of the files are easter eggs for your enjoyment.

Is this a hack sim? Is this an interactive digital novel? There are elements of both in this game, and I absolutely love it. I always felt like "ok, we have all of these commands at our disposal.... now throw a wrench in the gears and give us a new OS to hack" or something along those lines. In other words, the game does get repetative after 10 hours of gameplay, but that's grasping at straws for something bad here. I also found the network map very unintuitive near the end of the game with as many networks as there were, wishing I could have deleted some manually.

First things first, I loved the slick layout and visuals Hacknet plays quite nicely.  Music is pretty damn good too!

At first I really liked Hacknet as it feels like what Uplink should be in the modern gaming age.  You get cool looking interfaces, some psuedo-unix commands and maniplulations and a feeling of pressure as you hack your way past traces and logs.  However, thats where it falls apart a little.  You realise that logs are redundant and apart from an active trace when hacking some systems there are no repercussions to breaking log chains.  Except for one scripted event you dont need to worry about the men in black knocking on your door.  It was this attention to detail and consequnce that, in my opinion, gave Uplink its amazing gameplay.  I felt like the game needed that next level of complexity and difficulty to really come of age.

The major thumbs down however is game breaking bugs.  At time of writing this review there is at least one huge bug that is preventing the game being completed.  An attempt at fixing the bug was done but it did not solve the problem.  Cudos for the Developer at rushing to solve the issue but after one attempted patch there has been no communication on the status of the bug for about a month now.

Bottomline.  Its a fun little game but becomes one dimentional and easy once you realise there is no real way to lose apart from letting an active hack trace get you but even that is easily bypassed with one click or command.  The killer at this stage is bugs and more bugs.  I hope the game gets fixed and expanded, it could be a very nice game one day.


UPDATE:  The major bug has been fixed and I was able to finish the game.  Thanks to the Dev for fixing that up.

Awesome game! You are not actively modifying code like in Hack 'n Slash. Rather, you are typing in prompts within a command box in order to execute files/commands. You are also able to navigate using a point and click UI instead of having to type commands for every action you want to execute; however, commands are your best friend in this game.

Overall, if Watch_Dogs left you wanting more detailed hacking game play, then this will easily fill that void.

There are clear influences from Uplink, but Hacknet stands on its own two feet for many design decisions.

Hacknet requires a lot of typing due to the text console. This brings a level of realism which is enjoyable, and the countdown timers do not seem to require the player to type at 200 words per minute. However, a few actions can also be initiated by mouse using a graphical user interface. The use of the mouse is a bit incoherent: those features which can use the mouse and those which cannot feel arbitrary and without obvious design merit.

There are a number of little bugs here and there. Head over to the discussions and check the bug report thread. Many of the valid bugs reported actually have more to do with polish. It's unfair to call them bugs, but fixing the issues could enhance the game's polish and lead to better immersion. There are a few actual bugs that can lead to gameplay issues, but they seem to be few and far between.

The story is a bit linear. I have found it hard to explore the networked universe outside where the missions take me. Compare this to Uplink, where there are a great many ways to find and access computers by goofing around. Computers tend to have random snippets from bash.org , which are humorous logs of conversations that reportedly happened on IRC. It's a nice touch as a reward for looking at systems and it makes them feel a little more fleshed out, yet the contents tend to be disconnected from any of the game's context. The snippets simultaneously help and hurt immersion.

Creative expression is available in small doses, but I do not consider this any kind of sandbox game. The potential for such a thing is there. For example, there are computers which run web servers. You can modify the HTML, and when you visit the web server, your changes are visible. It can be amusing to deface a virtual server even if no other living being will see it. However, if you delete all the system files from a computer and then forcibly shut it down, it should prevent the system from rebooting. This would destroy a system. In Hacknet, if you do this, the system will disappear from your network map for a little while and then come back (while still lacking system files). As a related polish-bug: you can immediately connect to any computer "destroyed" this way using the command console, even if the network map does not show the system as online.

The music is electronica-themed to suit the stereotype of a computer hacker. The sound track brings good ambience. I personally start to notice the repetitious nature of the music after playing 2-3 solid hours, but that's usually a good time to take a break anyway.

The recent release for Linux/Mac is welcome, except that has introduced a number of new bugs that need to be squashed. Save game interoperability is a current problem that needs to be resolved at the time of this writing. Linux/Mac support has its own thread in the game's Steam discussion area. I'm sure those problems will be resolved soon enough, but they are worth reading through before purchasing if you plan to play on Mac or Linux.

Overall, I'd say Hacknet is a fun puzzle game with a solid computer hacker theme. It could use more polish and the design decisions regarding keyboard or mouse interfacing could use some rethinking. As a professional programmer and IT person, I cannot really say with certainty if this game is accessible to non-programmers or non-IT people. I suspect the game is approachable enough to anyone who has ever had to type commands into anything instead of clicking glittery UI buttons.

FULL:  This is a solid game that is easily worth the purchase price.  If you are interested in Dilbert comics, you will probably enjoy the humour in this game. I personally find the game acts as a refresher of sorts for the basic CMDs that we tend to forget in this GUI heavy age.  Yes, you may run into grammar and spelling errors throughout the playtime -but honestly, I feel that the communications that occur in this game, the ones you pick thru and piece together over several nodes, could actually take place.  The humanity in the conversations is there, errors and all, and I believe this is what draws the player in.  You do not lose complete focus on what you are meant to do, as much of your play circles around and ties upon itself.  If your current mission is not directly related to the main story, it is training for the next leg that will be taking place shortly. And there are actually very different ways to accomplish tasks!  Do you  delete and replace a file?  Rename it?  download it, modify, and reupload?  Which "group/faction" do you really want to participate with?  Did you fully explore all those IP addresses in the emails?  Gahh... I need to go back and play thru again!

Pretty fun 5 hour game. Some familiarity with terminals will make the early part of the game easier, but it is not required. The most fun I had in this game was recovering from "fail states" which were both creative and satisfying to complete. Story is well written, and kept me interested for the entire campaign. Game is well worth the price.

The way this game implements hacking does well to make you feel like a hacker without overly simplifying and abstracting what "hacking" is. The game has you sitting in front of a terminal scanning network security configurations for vulnerabilities and running exploits against a target. Obviously it takes a lot of creative liberties, you aren't getting into the weeds of researching CVEs or writing custom zero days, but you also aren't just pressing a random button on a phone to somehow take over city infrastructure as you'd see in a game like Watchdogs. It portrays hacking in a gamified manner without completely losing the surface level of what hacking is like in the real world, and the result is quite fun! Highly recommended.

"Uplink: Hacker Elite" was a fun game because it insulated the gamer from the tedium of command-line driven hacking. Hacknet attempts to do the complete opposite, by adding in copious amounts of esoteric Unix commands.

I only played the game for an hour before applying for a refund. The in-game emails that I read were mundane, as though this game was aimed at juvenile highschoolers ( I'm 40 years old ). One email was about a high school kid making out with a girl and prematurely ejaculating in his pants. Another email was a kid talking about the latest "Call of Soldier" game.

I had to do Google searches, to find out how to hack a firewall and basically gave up trying to figure out how to flood a proxy server.

I dropped out of programming school in real life. Programming & hacking can be quite tedious, which is why Hollywood and Uplink: Hacker Elite try and insulate the user from the realities of hacking.

I'd also like to point out that Uplink featured permadeath... which is where a lot of the tension came from.

This were one of the best invested 9 hours in my life. If you are a bit nerdy this is definetely what you want to play.
I've never seen hacking displayed so correctly in a game/movie ever before (I do know that this still isn't reality mind you ;) ). The game has humor, the story is tense (even though it's sometimes a bit cheesy) and the game is extremely in depth - ranging from
customized GUIs and ability to delete the GUI (while still being able to play the game)
over completly different storylines
to easter eggs.
And all that with real life UNIX commands. Mind. Blown. Now I just gotta get all the achievements and play the second storyline.

Hacknet is a great game for those of us that who grew up watching Hackers. While I can not say if this is a good representation of what it's like to hack a computer (as I have never even explored that avenue outside of trying to break into an ex's email in my youth) I can say that Hacknet is a very good representation of what I would imagine it's like to hack into computers.
The game's strength unfortunately, is also it's weakness.  It feels more real because there is no tutorial other than the information passed on naturally as you progress through the game. However, at times, especially after stopping and coming back to play, you could really use a refresher on what just happened.

My age might have more to do with this than anything else, but I also find it difficult to play long sessions of this game (even though I want to because I want to find out more in the story) my eyes, just get too blurry and tired.
I have yet to finish this game, but I plan on continuing it, just maybe after I look into some new eyes.

Overall: A nice little hacking simulation game that deserves a look over just as long as your eyes are up for the challenge. 

If you're still on the fence, I'd say just wait to try it when one of the Steam sales rolls on by.

Totally recomend this game to anyone. At a first glance this game seems like it would be boring but it is so addicting. Good length, took me 8 hours. it's cheap so pick it up. The logs you find on computers are hilarious to read. The story is pretty interesting. you get many new commands to use, and with the memory system it can be a challenge to get everything done in time. As for tips, always remember to eos-scan and scan if you are stuck, remember eos-device passwords, and unless given a username, assume admin is the username. Also, Forkbomb. 10/10 would recommend to a friend.

In Hacknet you take on the role of a rookie hacker who joins a group of hackers and slowy becomes better and better with access to better programs. It's tons of fun and absolutly hilarious if you read through some of the files. Keep in mind this game isn't at all a fast paced action game, but it completly makes up for that with some timmed missions that keep you on your toes. This is (in my opinion) one of the most interesting and intuitive indies out on steam and I definently recomend at least giving it a try!
